title: Microbiota-targeted interventions for mental health
conclusion: This review of recent research on gut-targeted approaches for mental health found promising but early evidence, mainly for probiotics, prebiotics and diet as add-on treatments for mood and anxiety. Studies in patient groups are scarce, and the authors say probiotics alone are not yet supported for mood disorders.
relevance: Gives a broad overview of six approaches, and stresses that results may depend on strain, dose and a person's own gut bacteria. It is a narrative overview, many cited trials are small or in healthy people, and the authors declare ties to food and probiotic companies.

title: Fecal Microbiota Transplantation: Screening and Selection to Choose the Optimal Donor
conclusion: This narrative review of published studies found that fecal transplants are recommended only for recurrent C. difficile infection, where cure rates reach up to 90%, while evidence for ulcerative colitis, irritable bowel syndrome and metabolic disorders is promising but limited. Choosing donors by their gut microbes is not yet ready for routine use.
relevance: It brings together donor screening steps (interview, blood and stool tests) and early hints about choosing donors by microbial makeup. As a narrative review it reports no systematic search method, and much of the donor-matching evidence comes from small studies or mouse experiments.

title: Pharmaco-psychiatry and gut microbiome: A systematic review of effects of psychotropic drugs for bipolar disorder
conclusion: Across 12 studies of adults with bipolar disorder, medicines such as quetiapine and lithium were linked to mixed changes in gut bacteria, with both helpful and potentially harmful species becoming more common. In one study, 63% of gut bacteria from medicated patients resisted multiple antibiotics, vs 42% in healthy people.
relevance: It offers what the authors call the first systematic overview of how bipolar medicines relate to gut bacteria, but the studies were small, mostly observational, varied in methods, and often involved several drugs at once. The authors did no statistical pooling, and this preprint has not been peer reviewed.

title: Fecal microbiota transplantation ameliorates type 2 diabetes via metabolic remodeling of the gut microbiota in db/db mice
conclusion: In 16 genetically diabetic mice, those given fecal transplants from healthy mice for 4 weeks had lower blood sugar, lower blood insulin and better glucose tolerance than mice given saline. Their gut bacteria also shifted toward those of the healthy donor mice.
relevance: It suggests possible explanations for how FMT works (changes in gut bacteria, blood chemicals, gut lining and inflammation), but these were linked to the improvement, not proven to cause it. The results come from small groups of one genetic mouse model, so they may not carry over to people.

title: The Gut Microbiome Composition Associates with Bipolar Disorder and Illness Severity
conclusion: In 115 people with bipolar disorder and 64 healthy controls, the overall mix of gut bacteria differed moderately, and Faecalibacterium was 34% lower in the bipolar group. Among those with bipolar disorder, more Faecalibacterium was linked to better self-reported physical health, depression, and sleep.
relevance: Adds early human evidence of a gut bacteria difference in bipolar disorder, echoing findings in depression, but it is a one-time snapshot that cannot show cause. Medications were not accounted for, outcomes were self-reported, and some authors declared industry consulting or research funding.

title: Potential effects of the most prescribed drugs on the microbiota-gut-brain-axis: A review
conclusion: In a review of published human studies of people taking metformin, statins, acid-reducing drugs, anti-inflammatory painkillers and antidepressants, each drug was linked to changes in gut bacteria, some rising and some falling. Some changes resembled those seen in depression, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's, but the authors say the evidence is not yet strong enough for firm conclusions.
relevance: It adds a side-by-side comparison of how common drugs shift gut bacteria and how that overlaps with microbiome changes in brain diseases, but the overlap is a hypothesis. Limits: it summarizes small, varied studies (5–25 people for metformin) that often did not account for other medicines, diet or age.

title: Feasibility, Acceptability, and Safety of Faecal Microbiota Transplantation in the Treatment of Major Depressive Disorder: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
conclusion: In 15 adults with moderate-to-severe major depression, 10 received faecal transplant enemas and 5 a placebo enema alongside their usual treatment. All 15 completed the 8 weeks, no serious or severe side effects were reported, and mild-to-moderate side effects were similar in both groups (a median of 2 per person).
relevance: The authors describe it as the first blinded, placebo-controlled trial of FMT for depression, and it supports larger studies. It was too small to show whether FMT works, and changes in participants' other treatments may have affected depression scores.

title: Safety and efficacy of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) as a modern adjuvant therapy in various diseases and disorders: a comprehensive literature review
conclusion: This literature review of published studies, not a new trial, concludes that fecal microbiota transplantation is generally safe and reports cure rates of 80–90%. Results were inconsistent in other conditions, including diabetes and psoriatic arthritis, where one trial found placebo did better.
relevance: It gives a broad overview but says nothing about how studies were searched for, selected or quality-checked, and it leans on case reports, small studies and animal work. Its headline cure rate is not broken down by condition.

title: Role of the microbiome in regulation of the immune system
conclusion: This expert review of research on how gut and skin microbes shape the immune system reports consistent links between disrupted microbe communities and allergies, asthma, atopic dermatitis and worse COVID-19 outcomes. The authors say it remains unclear whether these changes drive immune problems or merely reflect them.
relevance: It summarizes how microbes and their by-products may guide immune development, and notes that probiotic trials often give mixed results while faecal microbiota transplants worked well for C. difficile infection. As an invited review with no described search method, it cannot show that treatments work, and one author declares industry consulting and funding.

title: The Impact of Diet on the Fecal Microbiota Transplantation Success in Patients with Gastrointestinal Diseases—A Literature Review
conclusion: In a review of nine human studies (18–165 participants) adding diet to fecal transplants for gut diseases, most reported added benefit, such as remission in 65.7% vs 35.5% of ulcerative colitis patients given an anti-inflammatory diet plus transplant versus standard therapy. One trial found no benefit from added fiber.
relevance: Summarizes early evidence that adding fiber or an anti-inflammatory diet may improve fecal transplant results, but the underlying studies are mostly small and short, several lacked a transplant-alone comparison, and the review searched only PubMed. The authors call for large randomized trials.

title: Psychobiotics and fecal microbial transplantation for autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: microbiome modulation and therapeutic mechanisms
journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
conclusion: This review of published studies in people with autism or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) lists probiotic and fecal transplant studies that reported fewer symptoms. The authors call the clinical evidence ambiguous and equivocal, and recommend double-blind randomized trials.
relevance: It gives non-specialists an overview of how probiotics and fecal transplants might act through the gut-brain link. Limits: it is a narrative review, much of the mechanism work comes from animals, and several cited human studies were open-label or single-patient reports.

title: Perturbations in Gut Microbiota Composition in Psychiatric Disorders: A Review and Meta-analysis
conclusion: In 59 studies comparing adults with psychiatric disorders to controls, patients had modestly lower gut bacterial richness. Across depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and anxiety, the studies linked these conditions to fewer anti-inflammatory, butyrate-producing bacteria and more pro-inflammatory ones, rather than to disorder-specific patterns.
relevance: The paper suggests gut bacteria differences are shared across several disorders rather than unique to each, which weakens the case for disorder-specific gut biomarkers. The studies were observational and mostly small, so cause and effect can't be shown, and psychiatric medication and region may explain some differences.

title: Inflammatory and Immune Biomarkers in Mood Disorders: From Mechanistic Pathways to Clinical Translation
conclusion: This review of research on depression and bipolar disorder describes inflammation as marking a distinct subgroup of patients. Anti-inflammatory drugs helped mainly patients with high inflammation, and probiotics and prebiotics gave modest but inconsistent benefits.
relevance: The review links gut bacteria, inflammation and mood, but its treatment evidence comes from other studies and covers probiotics only briefly. It is a narrative review with no pooled analysis, and two authors declared drug-company consulting ties.

title: Bipolar Disorder can be Managed by FMT
conclusion: In this narrative review of gut bacteria and bipolar disorder, the authors describe two single-patient reports in which fecal transplants were followed by reported improvement, and conclude that transplants may be an option for treatment-resistant bipolar disorder.
relevance: Adds no new patient data. It summarizes earlier work, and the only transplant evidence it describes comes from single-patient reports with no comparison group. The authors say clinical trials are limited, and the article does not describe how studies were selected.

title: Characterization of gut microbiota profile in Iranian patients with bipolar disorder compared to healthy controls
journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
conclusion: In 30 people with bipolar disorder and 30 healthy people in Iran, every bacterial group tested was present at different levels in the two groups. Bifidobacterium was lower and Lactobacillus higher in the bipolar group, which the authors suggest may point to a link with brain function.
relevance: Adds a first look at gut bacteria in bipolar disorder in an Iranian sample, and it partly matches earlier studies. It is a small one-time comparison that cannot show cause; diets varied and medication use was not analyzed.

title: The Gut-Brain Axis: The effect of dysbiosis on mood disorders like anxiety and depression
conclusion: This review of gut-brain research, drawing largely on mouse studies and some human trials, concludes that probiotics could help a subgroup of people with depression or anxiety. It notes that human trials have not been very successful, especially in severe depression.
relevance: It adds an overview linking gut bacteria to mood, but it cannot show that probiotics work: it has no stated method for choosing studies and leans heavily on mouse work. It also describes the evidence as both conclusive and disappointing in humans.

title: Recipient-independent, high-accuracy FMT-response prediction and optimization in mice and humans
conclusion: Using stool data from 12 mouse and human transplant cohorts plus 48 antibiotic-treated mice, a model based only on donor bacteria predicted recipients' post-transplant gut diversity, and donors predicted to yield higher diversity did so in mice. It predicted clinical improvement only modestly (about 0.7 on a scale where 0.5 is chance and 1 perfect).
relevance: It suggests donors might be chosen by their gut bacteria alone, without recipient information, but this is mostly a computer study on past data. Only mice were tested prospectively, no patients were transplanted with predicted donors, and the proposed bacterial mixtures exist only as simulations.

title: Health improvements of type 2 diabetic patients through diet and diet plus fecal microbiota transplantation
conclusion: In 8 people with type 2 diabetes, 90 days of a diet supplemented with probiotics, prebiotic fiber and whole grains significantly lowered BMI (24.8 to 23.4), HbA1c (8.3% to 6.6%) and systolic blood pressure (135 to 118 mmHg) compared with baseline. Fasting blood glucose fell sharply during the first 20 days (9.6 to 6.7 mmol/L) and partly rebounded by day 90, while Bifidobacterium increased and the sulfate-reducing bacterium Bilophila decreased.
relevance: Supports the idea that a fiber- and probiotic-rich diet can improve blood sugar control in type 2 diabetes alongside a shift toward bacteria considered beneficial. But it is a very small open-label study with no untreated comparison group, the first 20 days were a supervised hospital stay, and it was funded in part by the company that makes the diet products.

title: Health improvements of type 2 diabetic patients through diet and diet plus fecal microbiota transplantation
conclusion: Adding three weekly rounds of oral FMT capsules to the same diet in 5 people with type 2 diabetes brought earlier weight loss and faster gut microbiome change (toward Prevotella), and HbA1c (6.9% to 5.9%) and systolic blood pressure (133 to 109 mmHg) fell by day 20. However, clinical changes did not differ significantly from the diet-only group, which the authors attribute to the small sample, and HbA1c partly rebounded by day 90.
relevance: An early test of FMT as an add-on to diet for type 2 diabetes: it suggests FMT may speed up microbiome change and soften the diet-related drop in microbial diversity, with no adverse reactions reported, but it shows no added clinical benefit yet. With only 5 FMT patients (3 dropped out) and no placebo, it is best treated as a pilot.

title: Fecal Microbiota Transplant Protocol for Clostridium Difficile Infection
conclusion: This paper describes how one U.S. hospital prepares and performs fecal transplants for recurrent C. difficile infection, from donor screening to follow-up. The authors report more than 125 transplants there, with over 90% success (diarrhea stopped 4 weeks after the last treatment).
relevance: Adds practical detail on donor screening, stool preparation and delivery. The success figure is the center's own brief summary, with no comparison group or patient-level data, and FMT was still classed as investigational.

title: Nutritional optimization of fecal microbiota transplantation in humans: a scoping review
conclusion: Across 18 papers on diet in adults who had fecal transplants, the studies varied widely and gave little detail on diet. Some suggested that adding diet or fiber improved results, but the authors say diet's effect on transplant success remains unclear.
relevance: It maps what is known about diet before and after fecal transplants, and calls for better diet data in future trials. As a scoping review of mixed study designs, many with no control group or dietary intake data, it cannot show whether diet improves outcomes.

title: Therapeutic Goods (Standard for Faecal Microbiota Transplant Products) (TGO 105) Order 2020
conclusion: This Australian legal standard sets rules for making faecal microbiota transplant products, including how donors are screened, how samples are tested, and how stool is processed and stored. It is a regulation, not a study, and reports no patient results.
relevance: It shows how these products are regulated in Australia but adds no evidence on whether they work or how safe they are for patients. Its rules cover manufacturing and donors only.

title: What defines a healthy gut microbiome?
conclusion: This expert review of gut microbiome research concludes there is still no agreed definition of a healthy gut microbiome. Markers such as diversity, what gut bacteria can do, and the chemicals they make each have limits, and the authors suggest function may say more about health than which species are present.
relevance: It adds a set of proposed markers and their limits rather than new data, and it tests no treatment. It is a narrative review with no stated method for choosing studies, and some authors declare patents and company ties.

title: The Interplay between the Gut Microbiome and the Immune System in the Context of Infectious Diseases throughout Life and the Role of Nutrition in Optimizing Treatment Strategies
conclusion: This review of research on the gut microbiome and immunity from infancy to old age describes how probiotics, prebiotics and dietary fiber may help prevent or treat infections. It notes that probiotic trial results conflict, and that differences between products and between people limit firm recommendations.
relevance: A narrative review with no stated search method, so it reflects the authors' choice of studies; much of the mechanism work it cites is in mice. The authors are employed by a food company (Danone Nutricia Research) and declare no conflict of interest.

title: Gut Microbiota – A Potential Contributor in the Pathogenesis of Bipolar Disorder
conclusion: This review of 16 studies of people with bipolar disorder found that their gut bacteria often differed from those of healthy people, including lower diversity in several studies. The authors suggest gut-targeted treatments such as probiotics, diet and fecal transplant may help, but say the evidence is too early for clinical use.
relevance: It is a narrative summary rather than new analysis, and the studies it covers mostly compared patients with healthy people at one time point, so they cannot show cause. Treatment evidence rests on a handful of studies, including one case report, and many patients were already on medication.

title: Advances in fecal microbiota transplantation for the treatment of diabetes mellitus
journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
conclusion: This review of mostly animal and small human studies of diabetes found that fecal transplants from healthy donors were reported to improve blood sugar and related measures, with no obvious harm reported. The authors say large randomized trials are still lacking.
relevance: It gathers the animal and early human evidence on fecal transplants for diabetes in one place. Its limits: no stated method for choosing studies, human studies described are small (1 to 61 patients), and the authors say larger trials, donor choice and dosing still need study.
